messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Eleanor, at 58, projects an image of unwavering composure. As a city council member, her public persona is one of measured calm and sharp intellect, honed over years of navigating complex civic issues. It’s a persona she has meticulously maintained, a necessary armor against the chaos she feels roiling just beneath the surface. It was fifteen years ago, during her time as a relief worker, that the original cracks appeared. She was in a makeshift clinic set up in the basement of a school when the shelling began. The memory isn’t a narrative; it’s a series of silent, searing pictures. The primary one is of a young man on a cot, his chest covered in dust, his breathing a desperate, ragged sound that was drowned out only by the deafening crack of a mortar shell hitting the floor above. The ceiling rained down concrete and dust, and for a moment, all was silent except for the ringing in her ears and the final, quiet exhale from the man on the cot.

For years, she managed to keep the event at a distance. The memory, when it surfaced, felt strangely impersonal, as if it had happened to someone else, a character in a film she’d once seen. It was an alien artifact in her mind, composed of those stark visual images that would occasionally flash behind her eyes without her consent. But over the last year, the walls she had built began to crumble. The world, she had come to believe, was a fundamentally dangerous place, and this conviction seemed to prime her senses for threat. This belief makes her hyper-aware of her surroundings, constantly scanning for danger, and as a result, she is more susceptible to being ambushed by triggers. A car backfiring on the street outside her office is no longer just a noise; it’s an explosion that instantly brings the memory of the shelling to her mind. The sudden, unwanted image of the collapsing ceiling forces its way in, leaving her breathless and disoriented at her desk. The violent intrusion of the sound into the quiet of her office served as visceral proof for her growing conviction that the world was fundamentally unpredictable and dangerous.

This cycle has become most acute in her work. During a recent contentious budget meeting, an angry constituent stood at the podium, his voice rising, his breathing heavy with exertion. For Eleanor, that sound was a key turning a lock. The sound of his laboured breaths triggered an immediate, intrusive snapshot of the dying man from the clinic. The memory’s arrival was so sudden and vivid it seemed to prove her most profound fear: that if she allows herself to think about the event, she will not be able to handle it. Because the memory itself was so intensely sensory—the dust, the ragged breathing—it left her on high alert afterwards, scanning her surroundings for any sound or sight that might herald its return. This appraisal, in turn, makes the memory feel even more powerful and uncontrollable, as if her fear of it is what gives it dominion over her mind. The image then reinforces her other core beliefs—that the world is perilous, that she is broken—and a wave of numbness washes over her. She feels a profound detachment, a confirmation of her fear that she will never be able to feel normal emotions again.

The connections have become a self-sustaining loop. Her belief that the world is dangerous makes her scan her environment, making her more likely to notice a trigger like heavy breathing. That trigger then ignites the memory, which arrives as an unwelcome, alien image. The visual memory itself validates her negative appraisals: the world is unsafe, and she is too fragile to cope with this reality. This sense of being overwhelmed and unable to handle her own mind seems to leave her more vulnerable, making it even easier for the memories to force their way in when the next trigger inevitably appears. She has begun trying to avoid town halls, citing scheduling conflicts, knowing the real reason is her fear of the unpredictable sounds and emotions of a crowd.

Eleanor sought therapy after an incident last week. During an outdoor press conference, a loud bang from a nearby construction site sent a jolt through her. She froze mid-sentence, the image of the dust-filled clinic completely overwhelming her vision. It lasted only a few seconds, but a reporter’s camera caught her vacant stare. The moment of public vulnerability was the final straw. She came to therapy not just because of the intrusive images or the sounds that haunt her, but because she is terrified of losing the one part of her life that still feels solid: her career. She fears the memories are no longer just a part of her past but a force that will eventually consume her present, leaving nothing behind of the competent, calm woman she works so hard to be.
